title: Kestrel and the ASP.NET Core Hosting Model
description: Understand Kestrel's cross-platform server architecture, how it compares to IIS and Nginx, and how to configure it securely for production workloads.

data.text: When you run a .NET web application, something has to listen for HTTP requests, accept network connections, and pass them into your code. In ASP.NET Core, that listener is a server. The default and most important server is **Kestrel**, a lightweight, cross-platform, event-driven HTTP server built into the framework.

Kestrel is not just a wrapper around an existing web server. It is an independent server written in C# that can run directly on Linux, Windows, and macOS. It handles raw TCP connections, parses HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, and pushes requests into the ASP.NET Core pipeline. Because it is built into the framework, it has first-class access to middleware, DI, and configuration.
ASP.NET Core supports two primary hosting models when running behind IIS or IIS Express. Understanding the difference is essential for diagnosing performance and memory issues in production.

data.title: Hosting model comparison
items: In-Process: The application runs inside the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe or iisexpress.exe). Requests bypass the ASP.NET Core Module (ANCM) proxy and go directly to Kestrel's internal components. This offers the best performance and lowest latency.

Out-of-Process: The application runs in its own dotnet.exe process, and ANCM acts as a reverse proxy forwarding requests from IIS to Kestrel over HTTP. This model was the default in ASP.NET Core 2.x and is still supported for compatibility.
Modern default: ASP.NET Core 3.0+ defaults to In-Process hosting on Windows. Out-of-Process is still available but rarely needed unless you encounter specific compatibility issues.

data.title: Why In-Process is the Default
data.text: In-Process hosting removes an extra network hop between IIS and your application. Benchmarks show meaningful throughput improvements, especially for high-latency payloads. The trade-off is that your code runs inside IIS's memory space, so crashes can bring down the worker process just like a classic ASP.NET application.

Kestrel is configured in Program.cs via WebApplicationBuilder.WebHost.ConfigureKestrel or by binding endpoints in appsettings.json. For production, you typically want to bind to specific ports or Unix sockets, set request size limits, enable HTTPS, and tune the thread pool.

data.text: When you use Kestrel behind a reverse proxy like Nginx or IIS, the proxy handles TLS termination. In that scenario, Kestrel listens on HTTP internally, and you should enable Forwarded Headers so your application sees the correct client IP and scheme instead of the proxy's internal values.

terms.definition: A cross-platform, event-driven HTTP server built into ASP.NET Core that handles raw TCP connections and HTTP protocol parsing.
ASP.NET Core Module, an IIS native module that proxies requests to the Kestrel process in Out-of-Process hosting.
A hosting model where the ASP.NET Core app runs inside the IIS worker process, removing the network hop to Kestrel.
A hosting model where the app runs in a separate process and IIS proxies requests to it over HTTP.
A server such as Nginx, IIS, or Apache that forwards client requests to Kestrel, often handling TLS termination and load balancing.

data.title: Compare Hosting Models
data.description: Document the hosting model used by your current ASP.NET Core project and identify the Kestrel configuration.
steps: Open the project's .csproj file and look for the AspNetCoreHostingModel property under a PropertyGroup for the IISExpress or IIS target.
If it is not set, determine which hosting model the project uses.
Locate where Kestrel is configured in Program.cs or appsettings.json.
Identify whether the app listens directly on ports or uses HTTPS with a certificate.
Write a short summary of how requests reach your application from the client to the endpoint.
data.expectedOutcome: You will be able to explain the full request path from client to endpoint and identify whether your app uses In-Process or Out-of-Process hosting.

data.title: Kestrel and Hosting Summary
points: Kestrel is the built-in, cross-platform HTTP server for ASP.NET Core.
In-Process hosting runs your app inside IIS, removing the ANCM proxy hop for better performance.
Out-of-Process hosting proxies requests from IIS to a separate dotnet.exe process.
Kestrel can be configured programmatically to control ports, HTTPS, request limits, and protocols.
Behind a reverse proxy, use Forwarded Headers to preserve the original client IP and HTTPS scheme.
data.takeaway: Kestrel is the engine of your ASP.NET Core application. Understanding its hosting model and configuration is the first step to running production-grade web services.
